questions.question: A cyclist pedals with a constant forward force of 150 N and travels 215 m along a slope. Show that the work done by the cyclist is about 3 x 10^4 J.
questions.answer: W = Fs = 150 N x 215 m = 3.2 x 10^4 J, which rounds to about 3 x 10^4 J.
steps: Work done by a constant force along its direction of motion is W = F x s.
The forward force and the 215 m displacement are both along the slope, so no cosine factor is needed.
32 250 J = 3.2 x 10^4 J, which rounds to about 3 x 10^4 J, as required.

questions.question: A 90 kg cyclist and bicycle travel 215 m up a slope at 4.0 degrees to the horizontal at constant speed, with a constant forward force of 150 N. Calculate the work done against air resistance.
questions.answer: Work done against air resistance = 1.9 x 10^4 J (about 19 000 J).
steps: Total work done by the cyclist is 150 N x 215 m = 32 250 J (from part a).
Height gained: h = 215 sin 4.0 degrees = 15.0 m.
Work done against gravity = mgh = 90 x 9.81 x 15.0 = 1.32 x 10^4 J.
Speed is constant, so kinetic energy does not change and the rest of the work goes against air resistance.
Work against air resistance = 32 250 J - 13 240 J = 1.9 x 10^4 J.

questions.question: State one assumption that must be made when calculating the work done against air resistance in part (b)(i).
questions.answer: Air resistance is constant (the same) over the whole 215 m, or there are no other resistive forces such as friction in the drive.
steps: The work against air resistance was found as total work minus work against gravity.
That subtraction is only valid if the air resistance force is constant along the slope.
It also assumes no other energy is lost, for example to friction in the bicycle drive.
So one valid assumption is that the air resistance is constant over the whole distance.

questions.question: At the top of the slope the road becomes horizontal and the cyclist keeps pedalling with the same 150 N force. Explain how the speed changes.
questions.answer: The speed increases, because the gravity component along the slope has gone and the forward force is now larger than the air resistance.
steps: On the slope, the forward force balanced the weight component along the slope plus air resistance at constant speed.
On the horizontal road there is no weight component along the road, so that part of the opposing force is removed.
The resultant forward force is now 150 N minus the air resistance, which is positive.
By Newton's second law the cyclist accelerates, so the speed increases.

questions.question: A 0.160 kg toy car starts from rest and reaches 2.6 m/s at the bottom of a slope. Calculate the increase in its kinetic energy.
steps: The car starts from rest, so its initial kinetic energy is zero.
Kinetic energy is Ek = 1/2 m v^2.
Increase in kinetic energy = 0.54 J.

questions.question: The car in Q2 does 0.26 J of work against friction as it rolls down. Calculate the vertical displacement of the car (mass 0.160 kg, kinetic energy gain 0.54 J).
steps: Energy conservation: GPE lost = kinetic energy gained + work done against friction.
Vertical displacement h = 0.51 m.

questions.question: A 50 kg box is pulled up a slope of height 2.0 m and length 15 m by a rope over a pulley, with an 8.0 kg mass falling and the box moving at steady speed. Determine whether the maximum efficiency is greater than 90%.
questions.answer: No. The maximum efficiency is about 83%, which is less than 90%.
steps: Useful output: the box gains GPE = mgh = 50 x 9.81 x 2.0 = 981 J.
Input: the 8.0 kg mass falls the same 15 m as the box moves along the rope, losing 8.0 x 9.81 x 15 = 1177 J.
Steady speed means no change in kinetic energy, and maximum efficiency means no friction losses.
Maximum efficiency = 981 / 1177 = 0.83, which is 83%, less than 90%.

questions.question: A 1560 kg car decelerates from 13.0 m/s to rest and 73.9 kJ is transferred to its battery. Calculate the efficiency of the regenerative braking system.
steps: Kinetic energy removed by braking: Ek = 1/2 m v^2 = 0.5 x 1560 x 13.0^2 = 1.318 x 10^5 J.
Efficiency = useful energy output / energy input = 73.9 kJ / 131.8 kJ.
Efficiency = 0.561.
Efficiency is about 56%.

questions.question: State how the drag forces on a car moving through air vary with its velocity.
questions.answer: Drag increases as velocity increases (roughly proportional to v^2 at higher speeds).
steps: Drag is a resistive force that opposes the motion of the car through the air.
As the car's velocity increases, the drag force increases.
At these higher speeds the drag is approximately proportional to v^2.
So a faster car must overcome a much larger drag force.

questions.question: Explain why the efficiency of the regenerative braking system varies with initial velocity, over 20 m/s to 40 m/s, as shown on the graph.
questions.answer: Efficiency falls as the initial velocity rises, and falls faster at high velocity, because the drag force grows with speed so a larger share of the kinetic energy is dissipated to the surroundings and less is stored in the battery.
steps: The efficiency is the energy stored in the battery divided by the kinetic energy the car starts with.
Drag on the car rises as velocity increases (roughly as v^2), so at higher initial velocity more of the kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy in the air by work done against drag.
So a smaller fraction of the kinetic energy is available for charging the battery and the efficiency decreases.
Drag increases faster than linearly with speed, so the fraction lost rises more and more rapidly: the curve is nearly flat at 20 m s^-1 and steepens towards 40 m s^-1.
Higher speeds also mean a larger braking power, so more energy is also wasted as thermal energy in friction and in the resistance of the wires and battery.

questions.question: A lamp with efficiency 0.68 usefully transfers 120 J. Which expression can be used to determine the energy E supplied to the lamp?
steps: Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, so E = useful energy / efficiency.
The efficiency is given as a decimal (0.68), not a percentage, so no factor of 100 is needed.
E = 120 / 0.68 = 176 J, which is option D.

questions.question: A crane lifts a container of weight 4.0 x 10^5 N through 25 m. Which expression gives the gravitational potential energy gained in joules? Options: A 4.0 x 10^5 x 9.81 x 25; B 4.0 x 10^5 x 25; C 4.0 x 10^5 x 25 x 9.81; D 4.0 x 10^5 x 9.81.
questions.answer: B: 4.0 x 10^5 x 25 J (the weight is already a force in newtons).
steps: The container's weight is given directly as a force in newtons, so g is already included.
Gravitational potential energy gained = weight x height.
Options A, C and D multiply by 9.81 again, which treats the weight as a mass, so B is correct.

questions.question: An electric pump has an output power of 25 kW and an efficiency of 52%. Which expression gives the rate in kW at which energy is dissipated?
steps: The useful output power is 25 kW, so the input power = 25 / 0.52 = 48.1 kW.
Power dissipated = input - output = 25/0.52 - 25 = 25 x (1 - 0.52)/0.52.
This equals (0.48 x 25) / 0.52 = 23.1 kW, which is option C.

questions.question: A proton and an electron have equal kinetic energies. The proton's speed is v and its mass is 2000 times the electron's mass. Which expression gives the speed of the electron?
steps: The kinetic energies are equal: (1/2) m_p v^2 = (1/2) m_e v_e^2.
v_e = sqrt(2000) x v, option A (the lighter electron is faster).

questions.question: A tractor pulls a trailer a distance s in time t with useful power output P. Which equation gives the force F of the tractor on the trailer?
steps: Power P = work / time = F s / t, so P = F s / t.
Rearranging, F = P t / s.
This is option B.

questions.question: A motor lifts a 50 000 kg mass through 25 m with an output power of 700 kW. Which expression gives the time in seconds to lift the mass?
steps: The useful work is the gain in gravitational potential energy: mgh = 50 000 x 9.81 x 25 J.
Power = work / time, so t = mgh / P.
The power must be in watts: 700 kW = 700 000 W, so t = (50 000 x 9.81 x 25) / 700 000 = 17.5 s. Option B.

questions.question: A machine has a power of 750 W and transfers 150 kJ of energy in time t. Which expression gives t in seconds?
steps: Power = energy / time, so t = energy / power.
The energy must be in joules: 150 kJ = 150 x 1000 J.
t = (150 x 1000) / 750 = 200 s, which is option C.

questions.question: An object accelerates from rest down a frictionless slope at 23 degrees to the horizontal, moving a distance of 20 m. Which expression gives its final speed?
questions.answer: C: sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 20 x sin23)
steps: There is no friction, so the only force along the slope is the component of weight, mg sin23; the acceleration is a = g sin23.
The object starts from rest and moves 20 m along the slope, so v^2 = 2as = 2 x 9.81 sin23 x 20.
v = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 20 x sin23) = 8.8 m s^-1, option C. (Equivalently, the height lost is 20 sin23 and v = sqrt(2gh).)

questions.question: The wind exerts a force of 225 N on a windsurfer, who moves 450 m at 40 degrees to the wind. Which expression gives the work done in joules? Options: A 225 x 450; B 225 x 450 x cos 40; C 225 x 450 x sin 40; D 225 x 450 x tan 40.
questions.answer: B: 225 x 450 x cos 40 degrees (about 78 kJ).
steps: Work done = force x displacement x cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the force and the displacement.
The force is along the wind, and the displacement is at 40 degrees to the wind.
The component of displacement along the force is 450 cos 40 degrees.
So the answer is B, since 225 x 450 x cos 40 degrees is about 77 600 J.

questions.question: A 90 N force pushes a 200 N box up a 10 m ramp onto a platform 4 m above the ground. Which expression could be used to determine the efficiency of the ramp?
steps: Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input.
The useful output is the gain in gravitational potential energy of the box = weight x height = 200 x 4 = 800 J.
The input is the work done by the pushing force = 90 N x 10 m = 900 J.
Efficiency = (200 x 4) / (90 x 10) = 0.89 (89%), option C. Options B and D wrongly add the two energies.

questions.question: A cyclist rides at constant speed up a slope. The vertical height gained is h, and the forward force from the road is F with negligible air resistance. Which expression gives the work done by the cyclist?
steps: The work done by the cyclist is the forward force times the distance moved along the slope: W = F s.
The slope is at angle theta and the vertical height gained is Delta-h, so Delta-h = s sin(theta), giving s = Delta-h / sin(theta).
W = F Delta-h / sin(theta), option D.

questions.question: A ball is dropped, bounces once and is caught. Which graph of gravitational potential energy against time could represent its motion?
steps: Egrav = mgh, so the graph has the same shape as the height-time graph of the ball (taking the ground as zero).
While falling from rest, the height decreases as h = h0 - (1/2)gt^2, so Egrav decreases with an increasing gradient (a curve), reaching zero at the bounce.
After the bounce the ball rises with decreasing speed, so Egrav increases with a decreasing gradient (a curve that levels off) until the ball is caught.
Graph A shows this pair of curved sections meeting at zero. B is one smooth arch with no bounce, and C and D have straight lines, which would need constant speed.

questions.question: A locomotive pulls a train at constant speed against a force of 8400 kN with output power 70 MW. Which expression gives the time in seconds to pull the train 1 km?
steps: At constant speed, power P = Fv, so v = P/F = 70 x 10^6 / 8.4 x 10^6 = 8.3 m s^-1.
That is option C (= 120 s); the other options do not convert MW and kN to the same units.

questions.question: A pump ejects 200 g of water per second from a hose nozzle at 3 m/s. Which expression gives the minimum output power of the pump?
steps: The pump must at least give the water its kinetic energy: power = kinetic energy per second = (1/2)(m/t)v^2.
The mass per second is 200 g = 0.2 kg per second, in kilograms.
Power = (0.2 x 3^2) / 2 = 0.9 W, option B.

questions.question: Explain why the kinetic energy of the hammer head as it hits the button is greater than the gravitational potential energy it loses as it moves down.
questions.answer: The person does work on the hammer head, so the kinetic energy at impact is the GPE lost plus this extra work.
steps: The hammer head's kinetic energy at impact equals the work done on it by the resultant force.
The resultant force includes the person's applied force, which acts in the direction of motion.
This applied force does positive work on the hammer head, adding energy.
So kinetic energy at impact = GPE lost + work done by the person, which is greater than the GPE lost.

questions.question: The hammer head starts at rest and a resultant force of 58 N acts on it over 1.2 m before it hits the button. The cylinder (mass 0.15 kg) must rise 2.7 m to hit the bell, and the efficiency of the energy transfer is 4.0%. Deduce whether the cylinder hits the bell.
questions.answer: The cylinder rises only about 1.9 m, which is less than 2.7 m, so it does not hit the bell.
steps: Work done by the resultant force = F x d = 58 N x 1.2 m = 69.6 J.
The hammer starts at rest, so this work equals its kinetic energy at impact.
Energy transferred to the cylinder = 4.0% x 69.6 J = 2.78 J.
Height gained h = E / (mg) = 2.78 / (0.15 x 9.81) = 1.9 m.
1.9 m is less than 2.7 m, so the cylinder does not reach the bell.

questions.question: If the velocity of the hammer head at impact doubles, the height gained by the cylinder does not double. Explain why.
questions.answer: Kinetic energy is proportional to v^2, so doubling v quadruples the energy transferred and the height gained.
steps: Kinetic energy E = 1/2 m v^2, so it is proportional to v^2.
Doubling v multiplies the kinetic energy by 2^2 = 4.
The energy passed to the cylinder is a fixed fraction of this, so it is also multiplied by 4.
Height gained h = E / (mg) is therefore multiplied by 4, so it quadruples rather than doubles.

questions.question: An object moving with velocity v has its kinetic energy doubled. Which expression gives its new velocity?
steps: Kinetic energy E = (1/2) m v^2, so E is proportional to v^2.
If E doubles, v^2 doubles, so the new velocity is sqrt(2) x v.
This is option A.

questions.question: A person holds a cable handle stationary by applying a force F of 121 N. The two sides of the cable make an angle of 60 degrees. Determine the tension T by a scaled vector diagram.
steps: The handle is in equilibrium, so the resultant of the two cable tensions equals F in magnitude.
The applied force F bisects the 60 degree angle, so each cable side makes 30 degrees with F.
F = 2T cos 30 degrees, so T = F / (2 cos 30 degrees) = 121 / 1.732.
T = 69.9 N, which a scale drawing also gives as about 70 N.

questions.question: A 150 N weight rises 0.25 m each pull; the person pulls 90 times in 120 s, and the machine displays an average power of 35 W. Deduce whether the displayed power is consistent with this data.
questions.answer: Work on the weight gives about 28 W, so 35 W is consistent only if the person's efficiency is about 80%, which is plausible.
steps: Work done per pull on the weight = 150 N x 0.25 m = 37.5 J.
Total work in 120 s = 90 x 37.5 J = 3375 J, so useful power = 3375 / 120 = 28 W.
The person's power input must be at least the useful power, so it must be 28 W or more.
The displayed 35 W is greater than 28 W, consistent with losses giving an efficiency of about 80%.

questions.question: Each litre of fuel releases 32 MJ. The car used 65 litres of fuel during an 8 hour journey. Show that the average power input to the engine is about 70 kW.
steps: Energy released = 65 litres x 32 MJ per litre = 2.08 x 10^9 J.
Average power input = E / t = 2.08 x 10^9 / 28 800 = 7.2 x 10^4 W.
This is about 70 kW, as required.

questions.question: The car travels 730 km during the 8 hour journey, with an average engine force of 2.1 kN. Show that the average power output of the engine is about 50 kW.
steps: Work done by the engine = F x s = 2100 N x 7.3 x 10^5 m = 1.53 x 10^9 J.
Average power output = work done / time = 1.53 x 10^9 J / 28 800 s.
Average power output = 5.3 x 10^4 W.
This is about 50 kW, as required.

questions.question: Determine the efficiency of the car engine, using the power input from part (a) and the power output from part (b).
questions.answer: Efficiency = 53.2 kW / 72.2 kW = 0.74, about 74% (about 71% if the rounded 50 kW and 70 kW are used).
steps: Efficiency = useful power output / power input.
Power output = 53.2 kW from part (b); power input = 72.2 kW from part (a).
Efficiency is about 74%.

questions.question: An electric pump lifts water 10 m at 4 kg/s and the water leaves at 5 m/s. Which expression could be used to determine the minimum power output of the pump in watts?
steps: The minimum power output equals the rate of increase of the water's energy.
Rate of gain of gravitational potential energy = (m/t) g h = 4 x 9.81 x 10 W.
Rate of gain of kinetic energy = (1/2)(m/t)v^2 = (1/2)(4 x 5^2) W.
Add the two: option C (= 392 + 50 = 442 W).

questions.question: State what is meant by a resultant force.
questions.answer: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on a body, found as their vector sum.
steps: Several forces can act on one object at the same time.
The resultant force is the single force with the same effect as all these forces together.
It is found by adding the forces as vectors, taking direction into account.
A zero resultant force means the object is in equilibrium.

questions.question: A boat has a constant engine force of 5.5 kN and mass 7.5 x 10^3 kg. At one instant the drag force is 3.1 kN. Calculate the acceleration of the boat.
questions.answer: Acceleration = 0.32 m/s^2 in the forward direction.
steps: Resultant force = engine force - drag = 5.5 kN - 3.1 kN = 2.4 kN.
Newton's second law: a = F / m.
The acceleration is in the forward direction of the boat.

questions.question: The boat's terminal velocity is 4.8 m/s. Calculate the output power of the engine (engine force 5.5 kN).
steps: At terminal velocity the resultant force is zero, so drag equals the engine force of 5.5 kN.
Power = force x velocity for a force along the direction of motion, P = Fv.
Output power of the engine is about 26 kW.

questions.question: A 72 kg passenger stands on a moving walkway on a 30 degree incline; the walkway speed is 0.51 m/s. Show that the rate at which the walkway does work on the passenger is about 200 W.
questions.answer: P = mg x v sin 30 degrees = 72 x 9.81 x 0.255 = 180 W, which is about 200 W to 1 s.f.
steps: The walkway lifts the passenger, so the rate of work equals the rate of gain of gravitational potential energy.
Vertical speed of passenger = v sin 30 degrees = 0.51 x 0.5 = 0.255 m/s.
Power = mg x vertical speed = 72 x 9.81 x 0.255 = 180 W.
180 W rounds to about 200 W to 1 significant figure, as shown.

questions.question: The walkway has an efficiency of 78%. Calculate the power input when 15 passengers of average mass 72 kg are standing on it.
steps: Useful power output = 15 x 180 W = 2700 W, using the power per passenger from part (a).
Efficiency = useful power output / power input, so input = output / efficiency.
Power input = 2700 W / 0.78 = 3460 W.
Power input is about 3.5 kW.

questions.question: A 7.2 x 10^5 kg train accelerates from rest on a horizontal track to a final speed of 76 m/s. Show that the useful work done is about 2 GJ.
steps: The track is horizontal, so the useful work done is the gain in kinetic energy.
This is about 2 GJ, as required.

questions.question: The train accelerates for 180 s with an input power of 16 MW. Determine the work done against air resistance during the acceleration.
questions.answer: Work done against air resistance = 8.0 x 10^8 J (0.8 GJ).
steps: Total energy input = P x t = 16 x 10^6 W x 180 s = 2.88 x 10^9 J.
Useful work (kinetic energy gained) = 2.08 x 10^9 J from part (a).
Energy balance: work against air resistance = input - useful work.
Work against air resistance = 2.88 x 10^9 J - 2.08 x 10^9 J = 8.0 x 10^8 J.

questions.question: Which quantity has SI base units kg m^2 s^-3? Options: A force; B momentum; C power; D work done.
steps: Work done has units kg m^2 s^-2 (energy, joules), so D is wrong.
Dividing energy by time gives kg m^2 s^-3, which is power.
Force (kg m s^-2) and momentum (kg m s^-1) do not match.
So the answer is C, power.

questions.question: A power station provides an electrical output of 2.1 GW and transfers thermal energy to the surroundings at 3.4 GW. Which expression gives its efficiency?
steps: Efficiency = useful power output / total power input.
The useful output is the electrical 2.1 GW; the total input is the electrical output plus the thermal power wasted, 2.1 + 3.4 GW.
Efficiency = 2.1 / (3.4 + 2.1) = 0.38, option A.

questions.question: A hydroelectric station has efficiency 32%. In one hour its useful energy output is 1.2 x 10^13 J. Which expression gives the total power input in watts?
steps: Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, so total energy input in one hour = 1.2 x 10^13 / 0.32.
Power = energy / time, and one hour = 3600 s.
Power input = 1.2 x 10^13 / (0.32 x 3600) = 1.0 x 10^10 W, option B.

questions.question: A 0.17 kg mallet moving at 1.6 m/s hits a stationary 0.035 kg disc. The mallet continues in the same direction at 0.3 m/s and the disc moves off with velocity v. Assume friction is negligible. Calculate v.
questions.answer: v = 6.3 m/s (in the same direction as the mallet).
steps: Friction is negligible, so the total momentum is conserved in the collision.
Initial momentum = 0.17 kg x 1.6 m/s = 0.272 kg m/s, since the disc is at rest.
Final momentum = 0.17 kg x 0.3 m/s + 0.035 kg x v = 0.051 + 0.035 v.
0.272 = 0.051 + 0.035 v, so v = 0.221 / 0.035 = 6.3 m/s. The kinetic energy rises from 0.22 J to 0.70 J, so the data are not physically realistic for a real collision.

questions.question: A 0.035 kg disc reaches the bottom of a 30 degree ramp at 5.0 m/s, moves 6.5 cm up the ramp and stops before moving back down. Determine the frictional force acting on the disc.
steps: Kinetic energy at the bottom: Ek = 1/2 x 0.035 x 5.0^2 = 0.4375 J.
The disc stops at the top of its motion, so Ek = GPE gained + work done against friction.
Vertical height gained = 0.065 m x sin 30 degrees = 0.0325 m.
Work done against friction = 0.4375 - 0.0112 = 0.426 J.
Friction F = work / distance = 0.426 J / 0.065 m = 6.6 N.

questions.question: A roller coaster car stops momentarily at P and then descends towards Q. Which expression could be used to determine the velocity of the car at Q?
steps: The car is momentarily at rest at P, so it starts with no kinetic energy.
The height drop from P (75 m) to Q (30 m) is 45 m, so (1/2) v^2 = g x 45 (mass cancels).
v^2 = 90g, so v = sqrt(90g), option D.

questions.question: A ball falls through a vertical height of 0.60 m before bouncing on a ramp. Show that its velocity immediately before the bounce is about 3 m/s.
questions.answer: v = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.60) = 3.4 m/s, which is about 3 m/s.
steps: The ball falls from rest, so energy conservation gives 1/2 m v^2 = m g h.
v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.60).
This is about 3 m/s, as required.

questions.question: Kinetic energy is conserved in the bounce, and the ball leaves at 70 degrees to the vertical. State expressions for the horizontal and vertical components of velocity immediately after the bounce.
questions.answer: Horizontal = v sin 70 degrees (about 3.2 m/s); vertical = v cos 70 degrees (about 1.2 m/s), with v = 3.4 m/s.
steps: Kinetic energy is conserved, so the speed after the bounce equals the speed before, v = 3.43 m/s.
The velocity makes 70 degrees with the vertical.
Vertical component = v cos 70 degrees = 3.43 x 0.342 = 1.2 m/s.
Horizontal component = v sin 70 degrees = 3.43 x 0.940 = 3.2 m/s.

questions.question: Point A is 0.86 m above the ground and 1.23 m horizontally from the foot of the ramp. Deduce whether the ball will bounce a second time on the ramp.
questions.answer: No. The ball lands on the ground about 1.8 m horizontally from A, beyond the 1.23 m end of the ramp, so it does not bounce on the ramp again.
steps: After the bounce the components are vx = 3.43 sin70 = 3.22 m s^-1 and vy = 3.43 cos70 = 1.17 m s^-1 upwards.
To fall 0.86 m below A to the ground: -0.86 = 1.17t - 4.905t^2, giving t = 0.555 s.
Horizontal distance = 3.22 x 0.555 = 1.79 m.
The ramp ends only 1.23 m horizontally from A, and 1.79 m > 1.23 m, so the ball has passed the end of the ramp when it comes down.
(Check: at x = 1.23 m the ball is only 0.27 m below A, but the ramp end is 0.86 m below A, so the ball is above the ramp.)

questions.question: State how the velocity-time graph shows that in 3rd gear the car has a smaller acceleration than in 1st gear.
questions.answer: The gradient of the velocity-time graph is the acceleration, and the graph is less steep in 3rd gear than in 1st gear.
steps: Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph.
The 1st gear section is very steep (about 7 m s^-1 gained in about 2 s, roughly 3 m s^-2).
The 3rd gear section is much shallower (about 5 m s^-1 gained in about 7 s, roughly 0.7 m s^-2), so the acceleration is smaller.

questions.question: Determine the average acceleration of the car while accelerating in 2nd gear, from the velocity-time graph.
steps: 2nd gear runs from the end of the dip after 1st gear (about t = 3.8 s, v = 6.9 m s^-1) to the peak before the next dip (about t = 10.6 s, v = 13.2 m s^-1).
Average acceleration = change in velocity / time taken.
a = (13.2 - 6.9) / (10.6 - 3.8) = 6.3 / 6.8 = 0.93 m s^-2, about 0.9 m s^-2 (readings from the graph, so accept a small range).

questions.question: Using P = Fv, comment on the magnitude of the forward force F in higher gears when the power P stays constant.
questions.answer: F = P / v, so F decreases as v increases; higher gears give a smaller force for the same power.
steps: Power P = Fv, so F = P / v.
With P constant, F is inversely proportional to the velocity v.
Higher gears allow a higher velocity v for the same engine power.
So the forward force F is smaller in higher gears.

questions.question: Calculate the minimum time for the car to accelerate from rest to 60 miles per hour, with 1 mile = 1600 m and negligible gear-change time, using the manufacturer's information.
steps: The shortest time uses the maximum acceleration in each gear: 1st gear up to its maximum velocity of 18 m s^-1: t1 = 18 / 2.9 = 6.2 s.
Then 2nd gear (maximum acceleration 1.2 m s^-2) from 18 to 26.7 m s^-1 (below the 2nd gear limit of 32 m s^-1): t2 = (26.7 - 18) / 1.2 = 7.2 s.
Total time = 6.2 + 7.2 = 13.4 s, about 13 s, with negligible gear-change time.

questions.question: Explain why there is a maximum speed at which the car can travel.
questions.answer: Resistive forces rise with speed until they equal the driving force, so the resultant force is zero and the car stops accelerating.
steps: The driving force from the engine is F = P / v, which falls as speed increases at constant power.
Resistive forces such as air resistance increase with speed, roughly as v^2.
The maximum speed occurs when the driving force equals the total resistive force.
At this point the resultant force is zero, so the car cannot accelerate further.

questions.question: A motor with efficiency 68% raises a 350 N load through 25 m. Which expression gives the energy supplied to the motor?
steps: Useful work = gain in gravitational potential energy = weight x height = 350 x 25 J (the load is already given as a weight in newtons).
Efficiency = useful energy / energy supplied, so energy supplied = useful energy / efficiency.
Energy supplied = (350 x 25) / 0.68 = 12.9 kJ, option D (the efficiency must be used as the decimal 0.68).

questions.question: A box is pulled 5 m along the ground by a rope at 40 degrees to the horizontal with tension 30 N. Which is the work done on the box? Options: A 150 J; B 115 J; C 96 J; D 23 J.
steps: Work done = F x s x cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the rope and the horizontal displacement.
Here F = 30 N, s = 5 m and theta = 40 degrees.
W = 30 x 5 x cos 40 degrees = 150 x 0.766 = 115 J.
Option A ignores the angle, while C and D use the wrong value, so B is correct.

questions.question: A rope at angle theta to the horizontal pulls a box a fixed distance s along a horizontal surface with constant force F. Explain how the work done by F varies as theta varies.
questions.answer: W = F s cos theta, so the work is greatest at theta = 0 and falls to zero at 90 degrees.
steps: Work done by a constant force W = F s cos(theta), where theta is the angle to the displacement.
Only the horizontal component F cos(theta) does work, because the vertical component does not move the box along the surface.
As theta increases from 0, cos(theta) decreases, so the work decreases.
At theta = 0 the work is maximum (F s), and at theta = 90 degrees the work is zero.

questions.question: A team pulls a 2.10 x 10^3 kg stone block up a ramp at a constant 0.450 m/s with total power 6.25 kW. Show that the total force exerted by the team is about 14 kN.
steps: The block moves at constant speed, and power P = Fv, so F = P / v.
This is about 14 kN, as required.

questions.question: The ramp has height 4.35 m and angle 6.0 degrees to the horizontal. Determine the total work done by the team.
questions.answer: Total work done = 5.8 x 10^5 J (about 580 kJ).
steps: Distance up the ramp s = h / sin 6.0 degrees = 4.35 / 0.1045.
Work done by the team = F x s = 1.39 x 10^4 N x 41.6 m.
Total work done = 5.8 x 10^5 J.

questions.question: Show that the useful work done on the block, which rises 4.35 m, is about 90 kJ.
questions.answer: Useful work = mgh = 2.10 x 10^3 x 9.81 x 4.35 = 8.96 x 10^4 J, about 90 kJ.
steps: Useful work done on the block = gain in gravitational potential energy = mgh.
This is about 90 kJ, as required.

questions.question: Determine the efficiency of the system using the useful work (about 90 kJ) and the total work done by the team (about 578 kJ).
steps: Efficiency = useful work done / total work done.
Useful work = 89.6 kJ from part (c); total work = 578 kJ from part (b).
Efficiency is about 16%.

questions.question: A trolley accelerates from rest at A down a straight track to B, with no air resistance or friction. Show that it reaches B with a speed of about 3 m/s.
questions.answer: v = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.50) = 3.1 m s^-1, about 3 m s^-1
steps: There is no friction or air resistance, so gravitational potential energy lost = kinetic energy gained.
The trolley falls through a height of 0.50 m: mgh = (1/2) m v^2.
This is about 3 m s^-1, as required.

questions.question: Determine the time taken by the trolley to move from point A to point C.
steps: Length of the slope AB = sqrt(2.0^2 + 0.50^2) = 2.06 m.
On the slope the acceleration is constant from rest to 3.13 m s^-1, so the average speed is 3.13 / 2 = 1.57 m s^-1 and t(AB) = 2.06 / 1.57 = 1.32 s.
On the horizontal section BC there is no friction, so the speed stays 3.13 m s^-1: t(BC) = 1.0 / 3.13 = 0.32 s.
Total time = 1.32 + 0.32 = 1.64 s, about 1.6 s.

questions.question: Explain how the counterweight affects the amount of work required from the electric motor to raise the lift.
questions.answer: The counterweight descends as the lift rises, so the motor only has to raise the net mass, and less work is needed from the motor.
steps: As the lift rises, the counterweight moves down, so its weight does positive work on the system.
The motor therefore only needs to raise the difference in mass, 2250 kg - 1300 kg = 950 kg.
The energy from the counterweight's fall supplies part of the energy needed to raise the lift.
So the counterweight reduces the work that the motor must do.

questions.question: The motor raises the lift 40.0 m in 30.0 s. The lift and people have total mass 2250 kg and the counterweight has mass 1300 kg. Show that the output power of the motor is about 12 kW.
steps: Net mass to be raised = 2250 kg - 1300 kg = 950 kg.
Power = work done / time = 3.73 x 10^5 J / 30.0 s = 1.24 x 10^4 W.
This is about 12 kW, as required.

questions.question: The motor dissipates energy to the surroundings at 3600 W. Determine the efficiency of the motor, given the output power of about 12.4 kW.
steps: Useful output = 12.4 kW; wasted power = 3.6 kW.
Power input = useful output + wasted power = 12.4 + 3.6 = 16.0 kW.
Efficiency = useful output / input = 12.4 / 16.0 = 0.78.
Efficiency is about 78%.

questions.question: A trolley of mass m runs down a slope from height h and stops over a distance d against a constant frictional force F on the horizontal section. Derive an expression for the gradient of the graph of d against h, in terms of F, m and g.
steps: The GPE lost on the slope equals the work done against friction on the horizontal part.
So mgh = F d.
Rearranging gives d = (mg / F) h.
The gradient of d against h is mg / F.

questions.question: Trolley A runs down the slope and collides with an identical trolley B at rest; they then move off together with velocity v. Assess whether the student's prediction, that friction being ignored, is correct.
questions.answer: The student is correct: v = sqrt(gh/2).
steps: Without friction, energy is conserved down the slope: mgh = (1/2) m u^2, so trolley A reaches the bottom at u = sqrt(2gh).
The collision is a joining (inelastic) collision, so momentum is conserved (kinetic energy is not): m u = (m + m) v.
v = u / 2 = sqrt(2gh) / 2 = sqrt(2gh / 4) = sqrt(gh / 2).
This agrees with the student's prediction, so the prediction is correct.

questions.question: A helicopter moves vertically upwards with increasing speed. Which option describes the increase in its gravitational potential energy? Options: A work done on the helicopter by gravity; B total work done by the helicopter; C work done by the helicopter against gravity; D work done by the helicopter to increase speed.
questions.answer: C: the work done by the helicopter against the force of gravity.
steps: The increase in gravitational potential energy equals the work done against gravity.
Option A describes work done by gravity, which reduces gravitational potential energy.
Options B and D describe total work or work that changes kinetic energy, not potential energy.
So option C is correct.

questions.question: An 8.2 kg object falls from rest through 25 m and reaches 20 m/s. Which expression gives the energy in joules dissipated by air resistance? Options: A 8.2 x 9.81 x 25; B 0.5 x 8.2 x 20^2 + 8.2 x 9.81 x 25; C 8.2 x 9.81 x 25 - 0.5 x 8.2 x 20^2; D 0.5 x 8.2 x 20^2 - 8.2 x 9.81 x 25.
steps: Energy dissipated = GPE lost - KE gained (energy conservation).
GPE lost = mgh = 8.2 x 9.81 x 25.
KE gained = 1/2 m v^2 = 0.5 x 8.2 x 20^2.
So the answer is C, the GPE lost minus the KE gained.

questions.question: Which is equivalent to 1 kilowatt-hour? Options: A 0.28 J; B 0.28 W; C 3.6 x 10^6 J; D 3.6 x 10^6 W.
steps: 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J, an energy unit.
Options A and B are wrong, since 0.28 is not the conversion factor.
Option D is a power unit, so C is correct.

questions.question: A 1.7 x 10^6 kg train moves up an incline through a vertical height of 25 m. Show that the gravitational potential energy gained is about 400 MJ.
steps: GPE gained = mgh.
This is about 400 MJ, as required.

questions.question: The train's engine has output power 20 MW and takes 35 s to move through the 25 m height. Calculate the work done by the engine against resistive forces.
questions.answer: Work against resistive forces = 2.8 x 10^8 J (about 283 MJ).
steps: Total work done by the engine = P x t = 20 x 10^6 W x 35 s = 7.0 x 10^8 J.
Useful work = GPE gained = 4.17 x 10^8 J from part (a).
Work against resistive forces = total work - useful work.
Work against resistive forces = 7.0 x 10^8 J - 4.17 x 10^8 J = 2.8 x 10^8 J.

questions.question: Explain why the equations of motion should not be used to find the maximum speed of a child sliding down a curved slide, with resistive forces ignored.
questions.answer: The equations of motion need constant acceleration in a straight line, but on a curved slide the acceleration changes in size and direction.
steps: The SUVAT equations assume constant acceleration in a straight line.
On a curved slide the direction of the child's acceleration changes continuously.
The size of the acceleration also changes as the slope angle changes.
So the equations of motion cannot be used, and energy conservation is used instead.

questions.question: A 24 kg child starts from rest at the top of a 1.7 m high slide and resistive forces are ignored. Determine the maximum speed v of the child.
questions.answer: v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 1.7) = 5.8 m/s.
steps: Resistive forces are ignored, so GPE lost = KE gained.
mgh = 1/2 m v^2, so v = sqrt(2 g h); the mass cancels.

questions.question: Slides X and Y have the same height, but X is longer. Child X has less mass than child Y. Both start from rest and resistive forces are ignored. Explain how the maximum speed vX compares with vY.
questions.answer: vX = vY, because the speed depends only on the height dropped, not on the mass or the slide length.
steps: Both slides have the same vertical height h and resistive forces are ignored.
Energy conservation gives mgh = 1/2 m v^2, so v = sqrt(2 g h).
Mass and slide length cancel out of the equation.
So vX = vY, even though slide X is longer and child Y is heavier.

questions.question: An engine transfers energy to water at 180 kW and wastes energy at 60 kW. Which expression gives its efficiency?
steps: Efficiency = useful power output / total power input.
The useful power is the 180 kW transferred to the water; the total input is 180 + 60 = 240 kW.
Efficiency = 180 / 240 = 0.75, option A.

questions.question: A cyclist moves along a horizontal road at constant speed, then at the same speed up a hill. Which graph shows how her power output P varies with time t?
questions.answer: D: power steps up to a higher constant value
steps: On the level road at constant speed, her power output is P = Fv, where F balances the resistive forces: a constant, non-zero power.
Going up the hill at the same speed, she must also supply a force equal to the component of weight down the slope, so the total force and the power P = Fv are larger.
The gradient and speed are constant, so the power is constant on the hill: a step up from one constant value to a higher constant value, graph D.
A starts at zero power, B increases steadily, and C steps down.

questions.question: An athlete of weight 680 N exerts a force of 890 N on the ground as he jumps. Explain, using Newton's third law, why he accelerates upwards.
questions.answer: The ground pushes up on him with 890 N, giving a resultant upward force of 210 N, so he accelerates upwards.
steps: By Newton's third law, the ground pushes up on the athlete with 890 N, equal and opposite to his push on the ground.
The athlete's weight of 680 N acts downwards.
Resultant upward force = 890 N - 680 N = 210 N, which is greater than zero.
By Newton's second law the athlete accelerates upwards.

questions.question: The athlete's weight is 680 N and his kinetic energy is 409 J as he moves horizontally over the bar. Show that his horizontal speed is about 3.4 m/s.
steps: Mass from weight: m = W / g = 680 N / 9.81 m/s^2 = 69.3 kg.
Kinetic energy Ek = 1/2 m v^2, so v = sqrt(2 Ek / m).
v = 3.4 m/s, as required.

questions.question: After passing over the bar with horizontal speed 3.4 m/s, the athlete falls a vertical distance of 1.4 m before landing. Calculate the magnitude of his velocity on landing and its angle from the vertical.
questions.answer: Magnitude = 6.3 m/s; angle from the vertical = 33 degrees.
steps: Horizontal velocity stays constant at 3.44 m/s, since no horizontal force acts after the bar.
At the bar he moves horizontally, so his vertical velocity starts at zero.
Vertical velocity on landing: v_y = sqrt(2 g s) = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 1.4) = 5.24 m/s.
Magnitude v = sqrt(3.44^2 + 5.24^2) = 6.3 m/s.
Angle from vertical: tan(theta) = v_x / v_y = 3.44 / 5.24, so theta = 33 degrees.

questions.question: Which unit is equivalent to the watt? Options: A N m; B N m^-1; C J s; D J s^-1.
steps: Power P = energy / time.
So the unit of power is joule per second, J s^-1, which is the watt.
Option A (N m) is the unit of energy, and option C (J s) is wrong.
Option B (N m^-1) is not a power unit, so D is correct.

questions.question: A moving staircase increases a person's gravitational potential energy by 5000 J in 42 s with efficiency 0.63. Which expression gives the power input in watts?
steps: Useful power output = energy gained / time = 5000 / 42 W.
Efficiency = useful power output / power input, so power input = useful power / efficiency.
Power input = 5000 / (42 x 0.63) = 189 W, option C.

questions.question: A car's brakes dissipate average power 50 kW from a constant frictional force F while it moves 13 m in 2.3 s to rest. Which expression gives F in newtons?
steps: Energy dissipated by the brakes = average power x time = 50 x 10^3 x 2.3 J.
This equals the work done by the friction force over 13 m: F x 13 = 50 x 10^3 x 2.3.

questions.question: A truck with kinetic energy 8.0 x 10^6 J enters a sand escape lane and experiences an average resistive force of 3.5 x 10^5 N. Calculate the distance moved by the truck on the escape lane.
steps: Work done by the resistive force = kinetic energy removed.
F d = Ek, so d = Ek / F.
The distance is about 23 m.

questions.question: The sand's resistive force is proportional to the vehicle's weight. Explain how the deceleration of a car on the escape lane compares with that of a truck.
questions.answer: The deceleration is the same for both, because the resistive force is proportional to weight and so to mass, which cancels.
steps: Resistive force F = k x weight = k m g, where k is a constant.
Deceleration a = F / m = k m g / m = k g.
The mass cancels, so the deceleration does not depend on the vehicle's mass.
So a car decelerates at the same rate as a truck, even though the car's force is smaller.

questions.question: Each pipe is 350 m long and inclined at 55 degrees. Each pipe transfers 1700 m^3 of water in one minute, with water density 1100 kg/m^3. Show that the power transferred by the water in each pipe is about 88 MW.
steps: Mass per minute m = density x volume = 1100 x 1700 = 1.87 x 10^6 kg.
Vertical height of the pipe h = 350 sin 55 degrees = 286.7 m.
GPE lost per minute = mgh = 1.87 x 10^6 x 9.81 x 286.7 = 5.26 x 10^9 J.
Power = 5.26 x 10^9 J / 60 s = 8.8 x 10^7 W, about 88 MW.

questions.question: Water passes through 4 identical pipes, each delivering about 88 MW, and the total power wasted is 256 MW. Calculate the efficiency of the power station.
steps: Power input from the lake through the 4 pipes = 4 x 88 MW = 352 MW.
Useful output = input - power wasted = 352 MW - 256 MW = 96 MW.
Efficiency = useful output / input = 96 / 352 = 0.27.
Efficiency is about 27%.

questions.question: A skydiver starts from rest and falls 11 m in the first 1.5 s. Air resistance is negligible if the mean acceleration is greater than 0.95 g. Deduce whether air resistance was negligible during the first 1.5 s.
questions.answer: Mean acceleration = 9.8 m/s^2, which is greater than 0.95 g = 9.3 m/s^2, so air resistance was negligible.
steps: Starting from rest, s = 1/2 a t^2, so a = 2s / t^2.
9.8 m/s^2 is greater than 9.3 m/s^2, so air resistance was negligible.

questions.question: Sketch the velocity-time graph for the skydiver between jumping and opening the parachute, using the displacement-time graph given.
questions.answer: A curve starting at the origin with steepest gradient (-g), flattening to a constant velocity of about -45 m s^-1 (downwards) by about 10 s, then a horizontal line at -45 m s^-1 up to about 21 s.
steps: The gradient of the displacement-time graph is the velocity. It is zero at t = 0, so the velocity-time graph starts from the origin.
The displacement graph gets steeper at first, so the speed increases; the velocity-time graph curves away from zero with a gradient (acceleration) that starts at about g and decreases.

From about 10 s the displacement-time graph is a straight line of gradient (-800 + 315) / 11 = about -45 m s^-1, so the velocity-time graph becomes a horizontal line at about -45 m s^-1 (terminal velocity), continuing to about 21 s.
Because displacement is measured downwards as negative, the velocity values are negative (below the time axis); they would be drawn positive if downwards were taken as positive.

questions.question: After jumping, the skydiver accelerated and then reached terminal velocity before opening the parachute. Explain how energy conservation applies to him before he opens the parachute.
questions.answer: GPE lost is shared between kinetic energy gained and energy dissipated by air resistance; at terminal velocity all GPE lost goes to the surroundings as thermal energy.
steps: Total energy is conserved: GPE lost = KE gained + energy dissipated to the surroundings.
While accelerating, part of the GPE lost becomes KE and part is transferred by air resistance to thermal energy.
At terminal velocity the KE is constant, so all the GPE lost goes to the surroundings.
The work done against air resistance is transferred as thermal energy in the air and the skydiver.

questions.question: The skydiver opens his parachute and his speed changes until he reaches a new terminal velocity. Explain how the forces on him cause his acceleration to vary after the parachute opens.
questions.answer: Drag becomes larger than weight so he decelerates; as speed falls, drag falls, so the deceleration reduces to zero at the new terminal velocity when drag equals weight.
steps: When the parachute opens, the drag force increases a lot and becomes greater than the weight.
The resultant force is now upwards, so the skydiver decelerates.
As speed falls, drag falls, so the resultant force and the deceleration both reduce.
Acceleration tends to zero when drag equals weight, giving a new constant terminal velocity.
By Newton's second law, a = resultant force / mass throughout, so the acceleration varies with the forces.

questions.question: An 1800 kg electric car moving at 14 m/s up a hill brakes to a stop. Its vertical displacement during braking is 0.76 m and the energy stored in the battery increases by 45 kJ. Calculate the efficiency of using the brakes to charge the battery.
steps: Kinetic energy at the start = 1/2 x 1800 x 14^2 = 1.76 x 10^5 J.
GPE gained while rising = 1800 x 9.81 x 0.76 = 1.34 x 10^4 J, which uses part of the kinetic energy.
Energy available to charge the battery = 1.76 x 10^5 J - 1.34 x 10^4 J = 1.63 x 10^5 J.
Efficiency = 45 kJ / 163 kJ = 0.28, about 28%.
